notes: The lamplighter of the Lantern Causeway (POI registry: 'lit each dusk by a lamplighter who sings as she goes'). The drowned climb the poles when she is not on the boardwalk (encounters/pois.json, unless_present).

greetings.text: You came along the boards in the dark. Then you came along them after me, and the light was mine, and you're welcome to it.
The singer of the round's back. Stand clear of the pole, I swing it wide.
I know the face. Isseva says it on the boardwalk now, which is how I know a face these days: the boards talk before the people do.

greet.speaker: Lissane Sa
greet.text: Mind the third plank from the Isseva end. It's been mind-the-third-plank for eleven years and the Council has a note about it somewhere. — You'll be wanting the light. Everybody wants the light, and nobody wants the oil, and nobody wants to be the one carrying the pole at dusk with the drowned watching from under the boards.

hub.speaker: Lissane Sa
hub.text: Well? The wicks won't trim themselves while I talk, but they'll wait.

choices.text: Why do you sing to them?
They say you're late on purpose.
Let me carry the jar to the next pole.

the_verses.speaker: Lissane Sa
the_verses.text: A verse is how long a wick takes to catch. Light one without and it catches crooked, and a crooked flame smokes the glass, and a smoked glass is a dark pole by midnight. — Forty years. I don't know how many lanterns there are; I know how many verses. If you asked me for a number I'd have to sing you the whole round to find out, and I'd lose count in the middle, and start again, and it would be dawn.

late.speaker: Lissane Sa
late.text: The drowned come up the poles. — The Reedfolk send their dead out with a lantern so the going-out has something to steer by, and sometimes the lantern goes out first, and what comes back up wants a light and a hand, in that order. They climb for the lanterns. You are only in the way. When every pole is lit they stay under the boards and hum. — After I've gone home the lanterns burn down one by one, and by midnight the poles are theirs. Cross early, or cross with a torch and a quick step.

on_purpose.speaker: Lissane Sa
on_purpose.text: Of course I am. — Isseva has a council, and the council has a memory like a reed basket, and a boardwalk that isn't safe for one hour of a restday keeps my name in their mouths and my oil on their account. Forty years, and they've tried to give the round to a boy twice. Twice the boy was late without meaning it, and that's worse, because I always come.

the_water.speaker: Lissane Sa
the_water.text: A lantern went out from the burial jetty on Tollday and it was still burning at dawn. They all go out by dawn; that's what they're for. The whole of Isseva's gone quiet about it, which is the loudest the Reedfolk get. — Don't take my word. Take the boardwalk to the jetty and look at the water.

carry.speaker: Lissane Sa
carry.text: Two hands on it, it's heavier than it looks, and don't swing it, fish-oil takes a week to leave a coat. — There. That's one verse I didn't have to walk for. The boardwalk will remember you did that, if nobody else does.

notes: The toll-keeper at the near end of the Chain Bridge (POI registry: 'a toll-keeper NPC'). A Rudd, because no clan keeps its own gate; Skardd ko-Skarl keeps the Kharrow end and counts the links.

greetings.text: Your name's on the slate. You went over and you came back. I'll wipe it.
Bridge is shut. Not locked; shut. Wolves have the far side after dark, and I go to bed so that I am not the one who let you over.

greet.speaker: Khath ko-Rudd
greet.text: Two marks and a name. The marks for the bridge. The name for the slate, and I wipe it when you come back over, and I have never wiped a name that did not.

paid.speaker: Khath ko-Rudd
paid.text: *(A hand flat on each of the four chains, in turn, the treaty order: Kharrow, Dreugh, Brindle, Ghast. Then the coin.)* — Good. That is the fourth and the coin comes after the fourth. Your name.

the_chains.speaker: Khath ko-Rudd
the_chains.text: Each chain is a treaty. Four clans hung this bridge, one chain each, forged by their own hands so the hands can be read off the iron afterwards. When a clan is shamed at the Moot its chain is loosened one link, and the bridge leans. — Look at it. It leans to the Ghast side. Everyone who crosses knows why, and nobody who crosses says, and I take their two marks either way.

the_count.speaker: Khath ko-Rudd
the_count.text: Skardd ko-Skarl, at the Hold end, on his knees on Kindleday with a hand on each link. Four hundred and twelve. — He has been out on the deck at night with a lamp this month, and a man does not count four hundred and twelve links by lamplight because he is sure of the number. Ask him. He will not tell you, and then he will.

wolves.speaker: Khath ko-Rudd
wolves.text: Crag-wolves. White, the year round, which on the far pavement is not a disguise, it is arithmetic: you count three and there are five. They come up the approach after dark and sit at the Hold end and wait for the bridge to bring them something. — By day the far side is yours. By night I would not cross for my own clan's chain.

notes: The knight in the eye of the Headless Watch (POI registry: 'The Order keeps one knight in the eye at all times. The current one has been there eleven years and asks for news of Tollmere prices.').

greetings.text: You've been to Tollmere. I can see it on you; nobody else walks that fast on ash. What is bread on the Row this month?
A sister of the vigil. Or a brother; the grey hides it and the Order is glad it does. Are you my relief? No. Nobody is my relief.
Quietly. The Choir rings the hours whether I count them or not, and I would rather count them.

greet.speaker: Calen Ash
greet.text: Stop there, and be welcome. The Order keeps a knight in the eye and the eye keeps a knight, and I am he, eleven years this spring. — What is bread in Tollmere?

hub.speaker: Calen Ash
hub.text: Ask, and I will answer, and then you will answer me.

choices.text: Bread's a mark and a half on the Row.
Why keep a watch in a stone head?
Has nobody come to relieve you?
There's another colossus on the heath.

prices.speaker: Calen Ash
prices.text: A mark and a half. *(He writes it on the inside of the eye with a burnt stick, under eleven years of other figures in the same hand.)* — Up a quarter since the autumn. That is the Tallymen and the barley both, and I would put money on which, if the Order let me keep any. — My mother kept a stall on Lantern Row. I know what bread is. I only want to know what it is now.

not_been.speaker: Calen Ash
not_been.text: Then you are no use to me and very welcome. Go to Tollmere; it is north, past the Mere, and it is loud. Buy a loaf. Come back and tell me what you paid.

the_eye.speaker: Calen Ash
the_eye.text: This is one of the Choir's heads. The night the note went wrong they came off, all twelve, and this one rolled further than the others, and somebody four hundred years ago cut a stair up its cheek and called it a watch. — From the eye you see the ring and the Seat and the whole heath to the Hushline, and a knight in the eye sees anything that walks toward the Seat. That is the vigil. It is not complicated. It is only long.

relief.speaker: Calen Ash
relief.text: I wrote every month for four years. Then every season. Then I stopped, because a letter that is not answered is a thing you have to carry up the stair and a knight is carrying enough. — The Ash counts twelve bells between noon and dusk. Some days I count eleven. I have written that down too, on the stone, where nobody will read it.

the_thirteenth.speaker: Calen Ash
the_thirteenth.text: Face down, a mile off the ring, as if it walked. — It has a head. I have sat in one of the twelve for eleven years and I know the inside of a Choir head the way you know your own mouth, and that one is not a Choir head; the brow is wrong and the Sayers who dig at it know it and argue about what that means instead of saying so. Keep clear of the diggings after dusk. The choristers go and stand round it and hold the note at it, and they do not like company.

bye.speaker: Calen Ash
bye.text: And you. Come back with a price.

notes: The hermit of Willow Isle (POI registry: 'a Tallymen clerk who stopped counting. He will tell you the price of anything, correctly, and refuse to sell it.'). Gives The Last Column (quests/side_2.json). His exercise book lies on his crate (encounters/pois.json, lies).

greetings.text: You've been to the Row. It's on your boots: Lantern Row mud is a mark a pound dearer than any other and it sticks like it knows.
Eleven hundred and some marks, on your belt, on an island. Don't sit near the edge.
Sit. The column's posted, in the only place it will ever be posted, which is a man's face. That was the price. It's paid.

greet.speaker: Ivo Goslin
greet.text: Four marks and a half, that coat, if you sold it on the Row today, and you would be cheated; five and three-quarters is its price. — Sit if you like. The stool is worth nothing, which is why I've kept it.

hub.speaker: Ivo Goslin
hub.text: Ask me the price of something. It's the one thing I'm still good for.

choices.text: Is there anything you want done?
What's the dearest thing in Tollmere?

the_isle.speaker: Ivo Goslin
the_isle.text: The willow, nothing: nobody can move it and nobody can sell what can't be moved, which is the one law the Tallymen never wrote down because they never needed to. The boat, eleven marks. The fish under it, more than the boat, fewer than the fisher thinks. Me, the Row wrote off at forty the year I stopped, which I thought generous, and said so, and they took two off for the saying.

stopped.speaker: Ivo Goslin
stopped.text: Twenty years copying the Ledger of Prices. Every line: what a purse is worth to the man who takes it, what a lie costs at the charter-board, what a name is worth to the Row when the Wardens strike it off their roll and nobody says it any more. — That one. I was halfway down the column for Mullbourne when I understood what the column was, and I put the pen down, and I walked out of the counting-house and kept walking until the water stopped me. — I finished it last winter. Out here. From memory. It adds up.

the_column_offer.speaker: Ivo Goslin
the_column_offer.text: Take it where I left it. — *(A single sheet from inside the book, folded in four, the ink twenty-two years apart down the middle of the page.)* — Orrin Quill is steward of the Row now. He posts the prices on the charter-board and believes it's the most honest thing in the city because it doesn't pretend to be free. Put that in his hand. And then come back and tell me what his face did, because that's the price I'm asking, and it's the only one I've ever set that I don't already know.

the_face.speaker: Ivo Goslin
the_face.text: Twice. Standing. — And then he sat, at the board, where a steward doesn't sit. *(He is quiet for the length of a column.)* That's more than I paid for it. — Here: nine marks and a half is what your trouble was worth, and you'll take ten, because I've never once in my life rounded down, and I'm too old to start on an island.

dearest.speaker: Ivo Goslin
dearest.text: Standing. — A barrow left standing in Lantern Row: forty marks, distraint, and the Tallymen will take the barrow as well if you're slow. Jory Wick's is still under it, I hear, from the boats that go by. Forty marks for leaving a thing where it was. I copied that line three hundred times and it was the one I laughed at, which tells you what sort of clerk I was.

the_book.speaker: Ivo Goslin
the_book.text: My exercise book, from the Row. I boxed my name out of the flyleaf the day I left; the rest I kept, because it's the only thing I ever wrote that wasn't a price. Read it if you like. It's about where you end and the world starts, which a clerk needs to know more than most. — It's not for sale. Nothing here is. Everything here has a price.

notes: A pilgrim who rests at Ansel's Hedge Shrine on some days (POI registry: 'a pilgrim NPC sometimes rests here').

greetings.text: You told her one. I heard it. She liked it; the hawthorn stopped scratching.
Sit if you're sitting. Ansel told stories about neighbours, not only the good ones. There's room in the chair for yours.

greet.speaker: Marigold Orchard
greet.text: Oh — sit, sit, there's room. The chair's Ansel's, but she never minded, and she hasn't said so. I was just telling her about my neighbour Bessa's grafting. You can listen, or tell her one of your own.

hub.speaker: Marigold Orchard
hub.text: The pie's for her, mind. The crust's for anybody.

ansel.speaker: Marigold Orchard
ansel.text: Hearth-Mother Ansel. She sat in this chair and told the first story about a neighbour, and the Vale says that's where neighbours come from: before her there were only people who lived near each other. The hawthorn took the chair over after she'd gone, the way hawthorn does, and nobody cut it back, which in the Vale is as good as a law. We bring a pie on Naming Day. I bring one every time. She's owed.

the_road.speaker: Marigold Orchard
the_road.text: The Ash. Pilgrim's Ash, to put on grey. Three years I've been walking it, and it's four days' walk, and that's because I stop at every shrine on the way for as long as it takes to tell the stone about somebody, and there are a great many somebodies. — The Ash isn't going anywhere. That's rather its trouble.

tell.speaker: Marigold Orchard
tell.text: *(She listens to the whole of it with her eyes shut, nodding at the places where a Vale person would nod.)* — There. She has it now. It's hers as much as yours, which is what a story told at a shrine is for: now it can't go quiet, because somebody who can't forget it has heard it.

the_news.speaker: Marigold Orchard
the_news.text: A pilgrim coming back the other way said somebody found the red poppy out west of the Choir, and ate it. Petals and all, standing in the grey. Nobody knows whether that was the Hearth in her or the Hollow. — I said the Hearth. She said I would say that, about anybody.

bye.speaker: Marigold Orchard
bye.text: Say hello to her on the way past. She hears.

notes: The day half of the Charcoal Camp's burners, and its merchant (POI registry: 'The burners buy anything that burns and sell gossip that does not. A safe camp with a job board.'). The camp's notice post is dressed by the builders when the encounter sentence mentions jobs.

greetings.text: You're up late, or I am. Barnaby's got the clamps. I'm only awake because the second one's fretful.
Buying, then. Nobody walks out to a burners' camp with that on their belt to sell me a twig.

greet.speaker: Sorrel Rooke
greet.text: Buying or burning? I buy anything that burns and sell what the clamps make. Mind your sleeve; the second clamp's fretful, and fretful turf takes a sleeve before it takes a hand.

hub.speaker: Sorrel Rooke
hub.text: Smoke says three hours to noon. Smoke's never wrong about the time.

choices.text: Why do you and your brother never sleep at the same time?
Is there work to be had?

the_clamps.speaker: Sorrel Rooke
the_clamps.text: Because a clamp left alone for an hour either goes out or goes up. Twenty-two years, Barnaby and me: I wake at eleven and he says 'wind's from the east' and I say 'is it', and he sleeps, and at three in the morning I say 'wind's from the east' and he says 'is it', and I sleep. It's the longest conversation either of us has ever had.

the_board.speaker: Sorrel Rooke
the_board.text: Post's by the fire. Charcoal buyers, hauliers wanting a hand, the odd body wanting a wolf thinned before they'll bring a cart up the track. They pin it there and I read it out to them when they can't. Take what you like off it; I get a mark off anyone who pays through the camp, which is my fee for the reading.

buying.speaker: Sorrel Rooke
buying.text: Wood, obviously. Cloth. Rope that's past trusting. Paper. Books — don't look like that; I've burned better books than you've read, and the better the book the steadier the burn, which is the one thing the Sayers and I agree on without either of us knowing why.

weather.speaker: Sorrel Rooke
weather.text: Rain by tomorrow noon. *(She looks at the smoke for a long moment.)* Or not. The smoke's right about the time and wrong about the weather half the days, and it's never told me which half.

notes: The night half of the Charcoal Camp's burners, and where its gossip comes from.

greetings.text: Mm? — No. Not asleep. Answering. Ask again, I'll be right either way.

greet.speaker: Barnaby Rooke
greet.text: Shh — no, go on, talk, talk. Sorrel's asleep in the lean-to and she sleeps like a clamp: quiet until she isn't. Sit by the fire. Everybody who comes past at night sits by the fire, and everybody who sits by the fire says something, and I hear all of it.

hub.speaker: Barnaby Rooke
hub.text: What'll it be — the talk, or the burning?

choices.text: What do people say round your fire?
Do you ever see your sister awake?

the_talk.speaker: Barnaby Rooke
the_talk.text: Fenwick Collier's clamp burned blue for an hour on Hushday night with the wood dry and the turf sound. Blue is copper in the ground or something older, and there's no copper under the Wold. He's banked it and he's not saying which. — That's the talk. The burning's all the same: slow, then all at once.

the_moot.speaker: Barnaby Rooke
the_moot.text: A hunter out of Fernhold sat where you're sitting a week back and said he'd seen the Hart standing in the middle of the Moot at dusk. Just standing, antlers up, the stones humming round it. He said it looked like it was waiting to be asked something. Then he said he'd not be the one to ask, and went to bed early, which is all you need to know about how it looked.

sister.speaker: Barnaby Rooke
sister.text: At three and at eleven, for as long as it takes to say 'wind's from the east' and 'is it'. Twenty-two years. — I know her better than anyone living. I couldn't tell you the colour of her eyes; they're always shut or they're watching smoke.

bye.speaker: Barnaby Rooke
bye.text: Quietly, going. She's fretful when she's woken, and so's the clamp.

notes: The One Poppy's sentence: 'a Hollow deed if picked, a Hearth deed if watered'. Put by the PoiTouch on the poppy (world/pois/poi_builders.gd, _strange_one_poppy); a conversation with nobody in it. A poppy picked sets poppy_picked, and the heath is built without it after that.

look.speaker: The One Poppy
look.text: One red poppy in a square kilometre of grey. Somebody has set a ring of stones round it and left a cup of water in the grass, and the ground inside the ring is trodden black by the people who walk out to look at it. It is the only colour for as far as you can see.

watered.speaker: The One Poppy
watered.text: The grey ground takes the water the way a dry mouth does. The poppy does nothing at all, which is what a watered poppy does. Somebody will notice the cup has been used, and say so at the Ash, and the Ash will decide what kind of person does that.

picked.speaker: The One Poppy
picked.text: It comes up easily. Four petals in your hand, and a square kilometre of grey with nothing in the middle of it but a ring of stones round a hole. The heath will know by morning.

notes: The look-out from the Wardens' Watch, the tower beside the Stair Head's way in the Choir's avenue (world/pois/poi_builders.gd, _wardens_watch): a conversation with nobody in it, put by the PoiTouch on the platform's far wall. From the Stair Head the heath's own ridge hides the country; from ten metres up here the first minutes see it, and this names what they see. From the Watch (-134, 3424): Merrowby 10 degrees at 2.1 km, the Cracked Toll 8 degrees at 2.3 km, the Grandfather 44 degrees at 4.1 km, Pilgrim's Ash 32 degrees at 0.6 km, the Wellspring 24 degrees at 0.9 km.

look.speaker: The Wardens' Watch
look.text: Ten metres up, the heath stops being the whole world. The Choir's headless giants still stand over you, and between them, past the grey, the country goes on green.

choices.text: Look back the way you came.

north.speaker: The Wardens' Watch
north.text: The green is the Vale of the Larkbourne. Where it narrows, two kilometres off, the roofs are Merrowby's, and the bronze above them, half in the hill, is the Cracked Toll. Nearer, still on the grey, is Pilgrim's Ash, and past it the Wellspring, where the green begins.

north_east.speaker: The Wardens' Watch
north_east.text: Four kilometres off there is a wood, and standing up out of it, higher than any tree has a right to, the Grandfather. There is a town inside it. At night, they say, you can see its windows from here, lit in the knots.

back.speaker: The Wardens' Watch
back.text: South, the Wardens' smoke on its knoll, the rim, and past the rim the mist over the Hush that you came up out of this morning.

notes: The hedge-witch of Foxglove Dell (POI registry: 'The hedge-witch Tansy Cresswell grows what Merrowby pretends not to buy. Something has been digging up her yew berries at night.'). Nell Harebell's cousin, at a distance: Nell's 'tansy' line sets heard_about_tansy, and this one's 'the_berries' sets tansy_yew_heaps, which Nell answers. Who takes the seed is left open, as the registry leaves it; the bristlebacks at dawn get the blame.

greetings.text: Door, not window. The window is for people who want to be able to say they only came about the weather.
Nell's told you about me and you came anyway. She'll have known you would; she tells people about me so that they will.

greet.speaker: Tansy Cresswell
greet.text: Mind the foxgloves. All of them: they're not for looking at, and neither am I. — You've come a long way off your road to stand in a ditch full of flowers. Buying, or lost?

choices.text: What do you grow out here?
Something's been digging up your yew.
Nell Harebell says you're her cousin.
Who comes all this way to buy?

the_dell.speaker: Tansy Cresswell
the_dell.text: Foxglove, which is a heart kept going in a thimble and stopped in a cup, and the whole of the difference is the thimble. Yew, for the same reason. And what the two of them make, in bottles, for the people who'll admit to buying. — The valley's dry, the hedge keeps the wind off and the sheep out, and nobody comes down here by accident. That's the other thing I grow.

the_berries.speaker: Tansy Cresswell
the_berries.text: Not digging. Picking. The boars come at dawn and turn the banks over and get the blame, because they're there to take it; but a boar would have the needles and the bark as well and die of it in the hedge, and nothing's died in my hedge. Somebody's been taking the berries, splitting them, keeping the seed and leaving the red flesh in neat little heaps under the tree. The flesh won't hurt you. The seed will. — Whoever it is knows which half is which, and wants the half that kills. I sat up four nights with a lamp. On the fifth I slept, and in the morning there were the heaps.

nell.speaker: Tansy Cresswell
nell.text: Cousin. Her mother and mine were sisters and didn't speak for thirty years over a wound wash, and Nell and I have kept the family custom up with a good deal less effort than they put into it. — We're not at odds. We're at a distance. She keeps her yew in a locked press and sells it to nobody, and I sell mine to anybody who asks me plainly, and between the two of us the village is served and each of us gets to be the one who was right.

buyers.speaker: Tansy Cresswell
buyers.text: Merrowby, after dark, with a scarf up, two hours each way to buy what Nell would sell them for a smile and a story about it in the Lip. Foxglove for an old man's heart. Something to make a long night shorter for somebody who isn't going to see the end of it. Something for a dog that has to be put down, for the man who can't. — I don't ask. I weigh it on my hand, and I tell them how much and how often and what it looks like when it's been too much, and they go home the long way.

bye.speaker: Tansy Cresswell
bye.text: Go out the way you came in. The hedge has opinions about the other ways.

notes: The gate-warden of Windgate at the Watch of the Gate (POI registry: 'The gate-warden takes a toll for a pass nobody can cross until spring, and spring has not come in years.'). A Dreugh: the clan that sits by the door at the Moot because it always leaves first (skerrow.json). What lies past the pass is hinted only, as WORLD_BIBLE §11 has it: the Ice Reach, a clan that went up and never came down, the giants' last road.

greetings.text: You're in the book. 'Crossed Windgate', it says, in my hand, and nobody in ten years has been able to say more than that.

greet.speaker: Ruska ko-Dreugh
greet.text: Three marks to cross Windgate. — You'll want to know the pass is shut. It is. It's been shut nine winters and this makes ten, and the toll is three marks, and for three marks I write you in the book as crossed and you may go up the road as far as the snow and look at it.

choices.text: Why take a toll for a pass nobody can cross?
When does spring come up here?

paid.speaker: Ruska ko-Dreugh
paid.text: *(She unwraps the book from its oilcloth, finds the page, and writes the day, your name and the word 'crossed' under nine winters of the same word in the same hand.)* — There. You've crossed Windgate. Very few people can say that these ten years, and every one of them paid me three marks to say it.

the_toll.speaker: Ruska ko-Dreugh
the_toll.text: Because the toll isn't for the road. It's for the gate. A Dreugh has kept this house since before there were seven clans at the Moot, and the duty came down to me with the name, and a duty that comes with a name you don't put down because the road's shut; you'd be putting down the name. — If nobody takes the toll, the gate isn't kept, and a gate nobody keeps is a hole in a hill. I've spent nine winters keeping a hole in a hill from being only that. At the Moot they sit us by the door because the Dreugh always leave first. Somebody has to be by the door.

beyond.speaker: Ruska ko-Dreugh
beyond.text: Snow, and under the snow the road, and the road goes up past the tops to the Ice Reach, where it runs wider and straighter than any clan ever built a road, and the old ones call it the giants' way and stop talking. — And a clan went up it once, one spring, all of them, and didn't come down. We don't say which. It isn't that we've forgotten. It's that we haven't.

spring.speaker: Ruska ko-Dreugh
spring.text: It came every year of my mother's life, and her mother's, and there's a line in the book for every thaw back to when the book was calfskin. Then it didn't. — The clans say the Breath is drawing in and the high places go first. The Sayers who came up to measure the snow said the note has slipped, and wrote it down, and went home before the weather did. I say it's been nine winters, and my brazier wants coal, and the book wants a line for today.

bye.speaker: Ruska ko-Dreugh
bye.text: Mind the road down. Nobody's fallen up this pass in ten years, and I'd like the book to go on saying so.

notes: First chair of the Sayers' dig at the Thirteenth (POI registry: 'The Choir has twelve. This one has a head, buried in ash, and it is not the head of the others. A Sayer camp digs here and argues.'). Holds that the head is the Cantor's likeness; Wennick Anthar holds that it was cut into the body afterwards; Calen Ash at the Headless Watch says the brow is wrong and the Sayers argue instead of saying so. Neither of them is shown right: the bible states no account outright.

greetings.text: You've been talking to Anthar. You have the look. He lies on the ash and says things at people, and they come away looking exactly like that.

greet.speaker: Gisel Morneth
greet.text: Mind the spoil. That heap is the last three days and I've been through it with my fingers twice. — You'll have come to look at the head. Everybody comes to look at the head. It is the Cantor's.

hub.speaker: Gisel Morneth
hub.text: Well? The light goes early on the ash.

choices.text: Anthar says somebody cut the face into it afterwards.

the_head.speaker: Gisel Morneth
the_head.text: The twelve are the Choir: twelve voices, cast to hold the note round the Seat, and when the note went wrong, the register says, their heads came off, which is why the Order has a knight living in one of them. This one lay down a mile from the ring with its head still on. — The Builders cast twelve for the ring and one for the Seat, and the one for the Seat was given a face, because the one who holds the note has to be someone you can look at. I won't say the name. It isn't said. But I have thirty years of rubbings from every Oroth lintel between here and the Mere, and I know that brow.

the_quarrel.speaker: Gisel Morneth
the_quarrel.text: Anthar thinks it was recut. Anthar thinks everything was recut, because his grandmother was a mason and he has her eye for a claw chisel and none of her sense. — Recut by whom? With what? And carried a mile from the ring and laid on its face by whom, and written down nowhere by anybody? He has an eye and no answers. I have an answer, and I will put my name to it, which is more than the Circle will let him do.

the_finds.speaker: Gisel Morneth
the_finds.text: Ash, mostly. A pilgrim's hand-bell with the clapper tied, under the ash against the hood, which means somebody sat down by this head on their way into the grey and left it here. — And the seam. We're down to where the neck meets the shoulders and there's a seam right round it. I say it's where the head was cast on. Anthar says it's where it was set on. We've been saying it at each other for a month, and the seam hasn't said anything.

the_night.speaker: Gisel Morneth
the_night.text: The choristers come after dark and stand round it and hold the note at it. We're in the tents by then with the flaps tied, which the Order would call cowardice and the Circle calls procedure; it's both. — They don't touch the dig. They sing at the head. I have lain in that tent and listened, and I'll tell you what I haven't told anybody at the Spire: I think they're trying to wake it, and I think they've been trying for a very long time. Be gone by dusk.

bye.speaker: Gisel Morneth
bye.text: Mind the spoil on your way. And if Anthar asks, I was civil.

notes: Second chair of the Sayers' dig at the Thirteenth. Holds that the face was cut into the head afterwards by somebody who wanted one particular face looked at, which is the design truth of WORLD_BIBLE §1.5 (being known holds) turned into a quarrel. Gisel Morneth holds that it is the Cantor's likeness. Neither of them is shown right.

greetings.text: She told you it's the Cantor's. Of course she did. She's been telling the head it's the Cantor's for a month, and it hasn't agreed with her either.

greet.speaker: Wennick Anthar
greet.text: Don't listen to her. — Sorry. You haven't said anything yet; it's a habit. Wennick Anthar, of the Circle: second chair on this dig, first on being right about it.

hub.speaker: Wennick Anthar
hub.text: Ask. Everybody asks, and then they lie down on the ash to look, and then they're on my side.

the_head.speaker: Wennick Anthar
the_head.text: Lie down. No, properly; get your eye along the stone. — The twelve were cut in one campaign by one school, and you could lay a straightedge along any of their brows in the ring and it would sit true. This one bulges over the left eye. That isn't a style. That's a person. Somebody came after the Builders and cut a face into a head of the Builders' stone: one face, somebody's, somebody they wanted looked at. And then laid it down a mile from the ring, where people would come and look.

the_quarrel.speaker: Wennick Anthar
the_quarrel.text: Of course she does. If it's the Cantor, it's the Builders', and the Circle can file it in the Oroth register next to everything else nobody reads. If it's a person, then somebody after the Builders put a face on fifty metres of their stone and walked it a mile from the ring, and the Circle has to say who, and how, and why nobody wrote it down. — She's right that I can't say. I'd rather be right and not able to say it than wrong and filed.

the_name.speaker: Wennick Anthar
the_name.text: 'Of the choir', in the liturgy. My great-grandmother took it off a lintel in the Undercroft because it sounded like money. It's the family joke that no Anthar has ever sung in tune. — So yes: I dig at the one colossus that isn't of the Choir, under a name that says I am. I've noticed. Morneth notices about twice a day.

the_night.speaker: Wennick Anthar
the_night.text: They come at dusk. Three of them, sometimes four, hoods up, and they stand round the head and hold one note until the sky goes white. We lie in the tents and argue in whispers about what it means, which is the only time Morneth and I whisper. — Don't be here for it. They don't care about the dig. They'd care about you.

bye.speaker: Wennick Anthar
bye.text: If you pass Morneth, tell her there's a mortar line in the seam. She'll say she didn't hear you. She'll have heard you.

notes: The Ash-Sweeper of the Choir road (POI registry: 'a lean-to of pilgrims' staves by the Choir road'). Gives The Swept Road (quests/the_map.json). His box gives up one thing each time the main line moves on: after The Toll Hums, What the Water Kept and The Held Note.

greetings.text: It's on the cairn, then. I went up and looked. I didn't touch it. — The road's quiet this morning.
I heard it. Down here, with the wind the wrong way, I heard it. — Sit by the fire. I'm not sweeping for an hour.
You've still got it. I can tell: you walk like somebody carrying a thing that wants to ring. — The box has something in it, if you want to look.
The note moved. The grey on the road moved with it, all of it, a hand's width towards the Choir, in the night. I've swept it back.

greet.speaker: Arn Sweeting
greet.text: Mind the pile, it's this morning's. — The grey comes over off the heath every day and lies on the road, and if nobody moves it the pilgrims can't see the waystones' feet, and they walk off the edge of the plateau looking for the next one. So somebody moves it.

hub.speaker: Arn Sweeting
hub.text: Ask, if you're asking. The broom doesn't mind.

choices.text: Why do you sweep towards the Choir?
What's in the box under the lean-to?
Has the broom turned anything up?
Is there anything in the box this time?
Is there something I could carry for you?

towards.speaker: Arn Sweeting
towards.text: Because the wind's from the heath and the grey comes with it, and if you sweep with the wind you're only moving it on to the next man. — That's the reason I give the Order. The other reason is that I stood a night with my back to the Choir, down at the line, and I'm not doing that again, not with a broom, not with anything.

came_back.speaker: Arn Sweeting
came_back.text: I was. Nineteen years ago this Ash Winter. Clean shirt, bell, the lot. I went down the Stair, and I stood at the line all night with the grey at my boots, and I listened, and in the morning I turned round and walked back up. — Don't ask me what I heard. Everybody asks. I tied my bell and left it on the cairn at the top like they all do, and the Order didn't know what to do with me, so they gave me a broom.

the_box.speaker: Arn Sweeting
the_box.text: What the road gives up. Buttons, mostly. Coins, which I put back in the waystones' bowls. A shoe, once, with nobody's foot in it. — And sometimes a thing that shouldn't be here at all. Those go in the box and I don't look at them again until somebody asks. Come by when things have changed out there. The road knows before I do.

find_pass.speaker: Arn Sweeting
find_pass.text: One. By the Glass Bridge, under a hand of grey, and the wax on it still soft. *(He takes a pass out of the box by one corner.)* A pilgrim's pass, stamped at every waystone. And once more after that. Count them.

find_page.speaker: Arn Sweeting
find_page.text: This. *(A page, dripping on his boots.)* It's been in the box a week and it's still wet. It came out of the grey on this road, and the grey is dry, and the nearest water is the Glassbed. — Take it. I'm tired of drying my hands.

find_count.speaker: Arn Sweeting
find_count.text: The morning after it moved. Face up on the road, pointing at the Choir, and the road swept clean all round it. Not by me. *(A count-card, the Order's kind.)* Cadwen says it's Toren's. Toren says it isn't. You tell me.

the_bell_offer.speaker: Arn Sweeting
the_bell_offer.text: There is. *(A hand-bell out of the box, clapper tied with grey thread.)* It came up under the broom this spring. It's been tied, so it came back up the Stair: that's the only reason anybody ties one. But the name round the lip is Tamsin Arle, and she's not on the Order's roll, and Cadwen's looked twice. — It belongs on the Turning Cairn, on the Stair's last bend, with the others. I don't go up there. You go.

choices.text: I'll take it up the Stair.

q_the_swept_road_back.speaker: Arn Sweeting
q_the_swept_road_back.text: *(He hears you out with the broom still going.)* Well. It's done, and it wasn't me that did it, and that's what I wanted. — I'll tell you a thing I haven't told Cadwen. The night I stood at the line there was a woman stood beside me the whole night, and in the morning she went on and I didn't. She had a bell. I never asked her name. — The box is yours, whenever the road gives something up.

bye.speaker: Arn Sweeting
bye.text: Walk in the middle of the road. It's the swept part.
